domain_title: Local Food and Family Farm Prosperity System
research_domain_title: Family Farm Wealth Engines, Local Markets, Regional Food Utilities, and Regenerative Stewardship
note: Major national doctrine complementing Community Food Security. Makes the local family farm a primary engine of community wealth, public health, land stewardship, and national resilience. Institutional purchase percentages (e.g., starting at 10%) are illustrative design parameters requiring modeling. Legal drafting 0%. Architecture ≠ evidence that Local Food Prosperity Funds or Food Utility Cooperatives already exist. Complements — does not replace — Community Food Security System.

central_promise.text: A farmer who produces healthy food, restores the soil, protects water, employs local people, and feeds the surrounding community should be able to earn a dependable middle-class or better income; build equity in the farm; pass the operation to the next generation; receive retirement and healthcare security; survive bad weather and market disruptions; compete without becoming a massive industrial operation; and share directly in the prosperity created by the local food economy.

goal.text: Build a profitable, regenerative local food system in which public purchasing, regional infrastructure, community investment, and environmental stewardship reinforce one another — not merely subsidize farms.

compact_language.text: The American Shared Prosperity Compact recognizes food, land, water, and soil as foundations of national security and community prosperity. We will rebuild a nation of locally rooted family farms by guaranteeing fair market access, investing in regional processing and distribution, rewarding land stewardship, expanding farm ownership, and ensuring that those who feed their communities share in the wealth they create. Our goal is a regenerative, low-carbon, naturally productive food system that strengthens farmers, nourishes families, restores the land, and keeps prosperity circulating within local communities.

farmer_message.not: We are going to impose new environmental rules on you.
farmer_message.is: We are going to make it profitable to care for the land, feed your neighbors, own your farm, raise your family, and pass something valuable to the next generation.
farmer_message.independence_rule: Provide choices, markets, infrastructure, and financial security — not replace one form of corporate control with government micromanagement.

scorecard_question.text: Is the land healthier, are the farmers more prosperous, are the people better fed, and is more of the wealth remaining in the community?

items.text: According to USDA ERS (America’s Farms and Ranches at a Glance, 2024 edition), family farms accounted for about 96% of U.S. farms and 83% of production value in 2023; small family farms were about 86% of farms but generated about 17% of production value.

According to USDA FNS 2023 Farm to School Census, SFAs participating in farm to school spent almost $1.8 billion on local purchases in SY 2022–23 — about 16% of their total food spending — and nearly three-quarters of SFAs reported at least one farm-to-school activity.

USDA AMS Local Agriculture Market Program (LAMP) and related local/regional market tools illustrate federal recognition of aggregation, distribution, and market-access infrastructure — not a finished Food Utility Cooperative design.

pillars.title: Local Food Prosperity Dividend
pillars.summary: County or regional Local Food Prosperity Funds invest in farms, processing, storage, markets, transportation, and food access; surplus shared among farmers, workers, local investors, hosting communities, and land/water restoration — ownership model, not temporary grants.

pillars.title: Local Food Purchasing Guarantees
pillars.summary: Public institutions purchase an increasing share from qualified local/regional producers when supply is available. Illustrative phased target may begin at 10% and rise as capacity grows — percentage requires modeling. Regional planners publish projected demand so farmers can plan before planting.

pillars.title: Regional Food Utility Cooperatives
pillars.summary: Farmer-controlled or publicly partnered shared infrastructure for processing, packing, cold storage, kitchens, aggregation, refrigerated transport, testing, branding, and ordering — the missing middle between farm and customer. Operate like public infrastructure with reasonable fees, not maximum extraction.

pillars.title: Farm Stewardship Contracts
pillars.summary: Pay for verified soil, water, habitat, drought resilience, and related public benefits based primarily on practices and measurable land improvement — not distant carbon-broker markets. Farmers keep control of land and future environmental value.

pillars.title: Regenerative Transition Guarantee
pillars.summary: Five- to seven-year voluntary transition support: partial income protection, transition finance, equipment/grants, technical assistance, early yield-loss protection, and premium purchase contracts. Public benefits of transition are not borne by farmers alone.

pillars.title: Regional Natural and Regenerative Standard
pillars.summary: Affordable, graduated recognition (Participating → Transitioning → Regenerative → Regenerative Plus → Regional Stewardship Leader) with farmer-to-farmer verification and transparent records — not bureaucracy only large corporations can afford.

pillars.title: Next Generation Farm Ownership Program
pillars.summary: Land access via long-term loans, down-payment help, shared equity, lease-to-own, tax incentives for sales to working farmers, conservation easements against speculation — tied to active farming and stewardship.

pillars.title: Rural Food and Farm Service Corps
pillars.summary: Paid apprenticeships, technical and business training, land-access help, debt relief, housing support, and prosperity/retirement contributions — connecting agriculture to broader service-to-wealth pathways.

pillars.title: Community Food Contribution Credit
pillars.summary: Extra incentives when food stays in the region (schools, food banks, markets, seniors, restaurants, CSA). Trade remains free; local sales should be at least as financially attractive as distant commodity markets.

pillars.title: Community Food Accounts
pillars.summary: Household accounts usable with participating local producers/retailers; additional contributions for lower-income, seniors, veterans, disability, and families with children; bonus value for qualifying local/regenerative foods without dictating diets.

pillars.title: Farm and Community Prosperity Accounts
pillars.summary: Retirement and healthcare security for participating farmers based on local production years, stewardship, community food supply, local employment, mentoring, and cooperative participation — succession without forced corporate or developer sale.

pillars.title: Protect independent farmers from corporate market power
pillars.summary: Rules against unfair contracts, retaliation, hidden pricing, processing concentration abuse, forced inputs, farm-data control, and discrimination. Right to repair; data ownership; transparent pricing; independent processing access; cooperative freedom.

pillars.title: Local Food Prosperity Scorecard
pillars.summary: Publish regional outcomes beyond commodity volume: family farms, farmer income, beginning farmers, family ownership acres, soil/water health, institutional local share, processing capacity, jobs, food access, succession, local circulation, waste/transport reduction.

flow: farmers invest in land and production
local workers earn wages and ownership shares
savings and public revenue return to the Local Food Prosperity Fund
the fund invests in more farmers, infrastructure, and community retirement security
economic_cycle.summary: A circular economy rooted in the land.

family_farm_prosperity_test.purpose: Screen agricultural, food-procurement, and rural-development proposals.
questions: Does the proposal make local family farms engines of community wealth rather than residual commodity suppliers?
Are institutional Local Food Purchasing Guarantees paired with published demand forecasts farmers can plan around?
Does shared Food Utility infrastructure fill the missing middle without extracting maximum profit from farmers?
Are stewardship payments based on practices and measurable land improvement rather than distant brokered carbon schemes?
Is regenerative transition voluntary, gradual, and financially supported?
Can small farms afford the natural/regenerative standard, or does certification favor only large corporations?
Does land-access assistance require active farming and stewardship rather than speculation?
Are Community Food Accounts increasing access without dictating household diets?
Do farmers earn retirement/healthcare security that enables succession without forced corporate sale?
Are independent producers protected from unfair contract and concentration power?
Does the Local Food Prosperity Scorecard ask whether land, farmers, people, and community wealth improved?
